title: Study identifies uniqueness of South Asian gut microbiome, critical for lifestyle disease treatment
body_text:
One of the largest and most geographically diverse investigations has found that South Asian gut microbiomes are distinct from those reported in other parts of the world and are shaped by local culture, diet, geography, and lifestyle.
The findings provide an important scientific foundation for developing microbiome-based diagnostics, personalized nutrition, and precision healthcare for South Asian populations, specifically for lifestyle disorders.
South Asia is undergoing rapid urbanization while simultaneously experiencing a sharp increase in obesity, diabetes, and other cardiometabolic disorders. Although urbanization is known to influence the gut microbiome, it was unclear whether these changes occur similarly across diverse South Asian populations.
Until now, most microbiome research has been conducted in European and North American populations, leaving South Asia largely underrepresented despite housing nearly one-fourth of the world's population.
Scientists from Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an autonomous institution of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) along with the University of Chicago, and collaborating institutions across India, Sri Lanka, and the USA, designed a study to understand how changing lifestyles influence the gut microbiome across different cultural, dietary, and ecological settings and to generate a comprehensive microbiome resource representing the diversity of South Asia.
Figure 1. Sampling locations across India and Sri Lanka.
They discovered that changes in the gut microbiome of each community follows its own unique microbiome trajectory shaped by local culture, diet, geography, and lifestyle.
Researchers collected stool samples together with dietary, lifestyle, and health information from 575 healthy adults belonging to ten South Asian communities.
Using the South Asian MicroBiome ARray ( SAMBAR)launched for the first time in India by the scientists of BSIP, the gut microbiomes of 575 adults from ten culturally and geographically distinct communities across India and Sri Lankawe analysed.
The gut microbiome was characterized using high-throughput DNA sequencing of bacterial 16S rRNA genes, followed by advanced bioinformatic analyses. The researchers compared rural and urban individuals within each community and also compared South Asian microbiomes with global datasets.
The project involved a large international collaboration among scientists from India, Sri Lanka, and the United States led by Dr. Niraj Rai, Group Head, Ancient DNA from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences, Lucknow. Field teams worked closely with local communities across India and Sri Lanka to recruit participants and collect biological samples and lifestyle information.
A community-engaged approach was followed throughout the study, with researchers sharing study findings back with participating communities. Laboratory analyses, DNA sequencing, and computational methods were then used to characterize gut microbial diversity and identify associations with geography, diet, urbanization, and metabolic health.
This approach enabled the team led by Shreya L. Ramachandran, Nagarjuna Pasupuleti, Richard J. Abdill, Niraj Rai and Maanasa Raghavan to identify both community-specific microbial signatures and common microbial changes associated with urbanization and metabolic health.
The study published in the journal Gut Microbes, highlights the importance of including underrepresented populations in global microbiome research. This is the first baseline gut microbiome data from India generated from the healthy individuals in India with huge medical and evolutionary impacts.
By demonstrating that different communities respond differently to urbanization, the study suggests that future microbiome-based therapies should be tailored to regional populations rather than adopting approaches developed solely from Western populations. The SAMBAR resource will also support future research on diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and other lifestyle disorders that are rapidly increasing across South Asia.
Publication link: DOI: 10.64898/2026.01.22.701183.

enrichment.summary: A study led by scientists from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP, under DST) and the University of Chicago, along with collaborators from India, Sri Lanka, and the USA, has found that South Asian gut microbiomes are distinct from those studied elsewhere in the world and are shaped by local diet, culture, geography, and lifestyle. The researchers analysed stool samples from 575 healthy adults across ten culturally and geographically diverse communities in India and Sri Lanka using a newly launched tool called SAMBAR (South Asian MicroBiome ARray), generating India's first baseline gut microbiome dataset. The findings, published in the journal Gut Microbes, indicate that microbiome changes with urbanization follow community-specific trajectories rather than a uniform pattern, suggesting future diagnostics and therapies for lifestyle diseases should be regionally tailored rather than based on Western population data.
enrichment.context:
Most existing gut microbiome research has been conducted on European and North American populations, creating a significant gap in scientific knowledge about South Asia despite it being home to nearly a quarter of the world's population and facing a rapid rise in obesity, diabetes, and cardiometabolic disorders linked to urbanization. This underrepresentation has practical consequences: microbiome-based diagnostics and precision nutrition approaches developed elsewhere may not translate well to South Asian bodies and lifestyles, given how strongly local diet and culture shape gut microbial composition.

The study is significant as a foundational, community-engaged research effort that generates an indigenous biological resource (SAMBAR) for future research into lifestyle diseases prevalent in India, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease. It reflects a broader push within India's science establishment, including DST-affiliated institutions, toward generating population-specific biomedical and genomic datasets to support precision healthcare rather than relying solely on data from Western populations, a concern also seen in initiatives like the Genome India Project.

prelims_questions.question: The 'SAMBAR' (South Asian MicroBiome ARray), mentioned in news for enabling gut microbiome studies, was launched by which institution?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that SAMBAR was launched for the first time in India by scientists of the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding a recent study on South Asian gut microbiomes:
1. It found that South Asian gut microbiomes are similar to those reported in European and North American populations.
2. It found that different South Asian communities show distinct, community-specific microbiome trajectories in response to urbanization.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: The study found South Asian gut microbiomes to be distinct from those in other parts of the world, not similar, and showed that each community follows its own unique microbiome trajectory shaped by local culture, diet, geography and lifestyle.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of generating population-specific biomedical datasets, such as the recently developed South Asian gut microbiome resource, for India's healthcare and public health policy.

India is witnessing a rapid rise in lifestyle diseases alongside urbanization. Examine how region-specific scientific research, rather than reliance on data from Western populations, can improve diagnosis and treatment strategies for such diseases.

study_notes.reason: The release names a specific institution, tool, and dataset (BSIP under DST, SAMBAR, first Indian baseline gut microbiome data) that is directly testable, while also carrying a clear analytical argument about why Western-derived microbiome science does not translate to South Asia and what this means for precision healthcare policy.

prelims.point: Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), Lucknow is an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology (DST)
prelims.why_important: BSIP's parent ministry/department is a classic factual pairing UPSC tests for DST-affiliated autonomous bodies.

prelims.point: SAMBAR (South Asian MicroBiome ARray) is a newly launched tool used to analyse South Asian gut microbiomes, first used in India by BSIP scientists
prelims.why_important: A newly launched, named scientific resource/tool is exactly the kind of specific factual item UPSC uses in 'which of the following statements is correct' questions.

prelims.point: The study analysed stool samples from 575 healthy adults across ten culturally and geographically distinct communities in India and Sri Lanka using 16S rRNA gene sequencing
prelims.why_important: Specific sample size, geographic scope and the sequencing technique (16S rRNA) could appear as a factual detail in a statement-based question.

prelims.point: This is India's first baseline gut microbiome dataset generated from healthy individuals
prelims.why_important: The 'first-of-its-kind' claim is a favourite UPSC testable fact, akin to first indigenous genomic/biological databases.

prelims.point: The study was published in the journal Gut Microbes, led by Dr. Niraj Rai of BSIP in collaboration with the University of Chicago
prelims.why_important: Attribution of a study to a specific researcher/institution and journal is a standard factual detail UPSC may test.

mains.point: Most global gut microbiome research has been conducted on European and North American populations, creating a scientific gap for South Asia despite it holding nearly a quarter of the world's population
mains.analytical_use: Useful for answers on why India needs indigenous scientific/genomic datasets rather than relying on Western research, paralleling debates on Genome India Project and precision medicine.

mains.point: Gut microbiome changes with urbanization follow community-specific trajectories rather than a single uniform pattern
mains.analytical_use: Supports 'discuss the health implications of urbanization' type questions, showing biological responses to lifestyle change are not homogeneous and need localized study.

mains.point: Diagnostics and precision nutrition approaches developed from Western populations may not translate well to South Asian bodies due to distinct diet, culture, and lifestyle-shaped microbiomes
mains.analytical_use: Can be deployed in 'critically examine the need for population-specific healthcare research in India' type questions, linking to affordability and appropriateness of imported medical technologies.

mains.point: Rising urbanization in South Asia is linked to a sharp increase in obesity, diabetes, and cardiometabolic disorders, and microbiome research could inform future therapies for these lifestyle diseases
mains.analytical_use: Provides evidence for questions on India's growing non-communicable disease burden and the role of scientific research in addressing it.

mains.point: The study followed a community-engaged approach, sharing findings back with participating communities during data collection
mains.analytical_use: Can support answers on ethical practices in biomedical/genomic research involving human subjects and indigenous communities.
